title: Historical stock prices and crypto quotes API in 10 lines of Python
author: ByteHarvester
summary: Disclosure: I built the Apify Actor used in this tutorial. This post was written with AI assistance. You want today's price for a handful of tickers, a year of daily closes for a backtest, and the sector and margins for a screen, without signing up for three different market-data plans. The Yahoo Finance Scraper ( highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes ) on Apify returns all three for stocks on any exchange, ETFs, crypto, currencies and indexes, from a single input, for $1.00 per 1,000 symbols on the free Apify plan. Price history and company data cost nothing extra. Here is the ten-line version, then the options, then a small portfolio report you can run after the close every day. The 10 lines from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run = client . actor ( " highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes " ). call ( run_input = { " symbols " : [ " AAPL " , " VOD.L " , " SAP.DE " , " SPY " , " BTC-USD " , " EURUSD=X " , " ^GSPC " ]} ) for q in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): if q . get ( " price " ) is None : continue print ( f ' { q [ " symbol " ] : < 9 } { q [ " price " ] : > 12 ,. 2 f } { q . get ( " changePercent " ) or 0 : + 6.2 f } % { q [ " currency " ] } { q [ " exchange " ] } ' ) Symbols are written exactly as Yahoo Finance writes them: VOD.L for London, SAP.DE for Xetra, 7203.T for Tokyo, BTC-USD for Bitcoin, EURUSD=X for a currency pair, GC=F for gold futures and ^GSPC for the S&P 500. Quotes come 50 symbols to a request, so a 300-symbol watchlist is a handful of requests rather than 300. A symbol Yahoo does not know comes back as a free record with error set and no price , which is why the loop skips those. Each record carries the full quote: price , change , changePercent , previousClose , open , dayLow , dayHigh , volume , bid , ask , marketTime and marketState , the ranges fiftyTwoWeekLow , fiftyTwoWeekHigh , fiftyDayAverage and twoHundredDayAverage , valuation fields marketCap , trailingPE , forwardPE , epsTrailingTwelveMonths and priceToBook , and dividendRate , dividendYield , dividendDate , earningsDate and analystRating . exchangeDelayMinutes tells you whether the quote is real-time or delayed for that exchange. Option 1: price history Set includeHistory: true and pick a range and interval. historyRange takes 1d , 5d , 1mo , 3mo , 6mo , 1y , 2y , 5y , 10y , ytd or max ; historyInterval takes 1m , 5m , 15m , 30m , 60m , 1d , 1wk or 1mo , with minute intervals available for recent days only. Exact dates go in historyFrom and historyTo as YYYY-MM-DD and override the range. The history lands in history.points , a list of {date, open, high, low, close, adjClose, volume} , plus history.dividends and history.splits . run = client . actor ( " highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes " ). call ( run_input = { " symbols " : [ " AAPL " , " BTC-USD " ], " includeHistory " : True , " historyRange " : " 1y " , " historyInterval " : " 1d " , }) for q in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): points = q . get ( " history " , {}). get ( " points " ) or [] if not points : continue first , last = points [ 0 ], points [ - 1 ] total_return = ( last [ " adjClose " ] / first [ " adjClose " ] - 1 ) * 100 print ( f ' { q [ " symbol " ] } : { len ( points ) } days, { first [ " date " ] } to { last [ " date " ] } , ' f ' { total_return : + . 1 f } % total return, { len ( q [ " history " ]. get ( " dividends " ) or []) } dividends ' ) If you work in pandas, pd.DataFrame(points).set_index("date") gives you a frame per symbol. Dividends and splits are already applied in adjClose , so return maths uses that column; close is the raw print. For a growing local archive, store the last date you have per symbol and pass it as historyFrom on the next run, so each day fetches only the missing points. Intraday work uses the minute intervals with a short range such as 5d ; Yahoo keeps minute bars for recent days only, so archive them as you go if you need them later. Option 2: company data includeFundamentals: true adds three objects per symbol: profile (sector, industry, website, employees, business summary), financials (revenue, growth, margins, EBITDA, cash, debt, free cash flow, ROE, analyst targets and recommendation) and keyStatistics (enterprise value, beta, PEG, short interest). Crypto, currencies and indexes are not companies, so they say so in fundamentalsUnavailable instead of returning empty objects. run = client . actor ( " highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes " ). call ( run_input = { " symbols " : [ " AAPL " , " SAP.DE " , " BTC-USD " ], " includeFundamentals " : True , }) for q in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): if q . get ( " fundamentalsUnavailable " ): print ( q [ " symbol " ], " - " , q [ " fundamentalsUnavailable " ]) continue p , f = q . get ( " profile " ) or {}, q . get ( " financials " ) or {} print ( q [ " symbol " ], p . get ( " sector " ), " / " , p . get ( " industry " ), " | margins: " , f . get ( " profitMargins " ), " | target: " , f . get ( " targetMeanPrice " ), " | rec: " , f . get ( " recommendationKey " )) The inner keys of financials and keyStatistics follow Yahoo's own names, so print one record once with json.dumps(q, indent=2) to see exactly which fields your symbols carry before you build a screen on them. A small portfolio report Put the holdings in a dict, fetch one run, and print value, day change and weight. This is the script to schedule after the close: HOLDINGS = { " AAPL " : 25 , " SAP.DE " : 40 , " SPY " : 10 , " BTC-USD " : 0.15 , " VOD.L " : 500 } run = client . actor ( " highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes " ). call ( run_input = { " symbols " : list ( HOLDINGS )} ) rows = [] for q in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): if q . get ( " price " ) is None : continue qty = HOLDINGS [ q [ " symbol " ]] rows . append ({ " symbol " : q [ " symbol " ], " currency " : q [ " currency " ], " qty " : qty , " price " : q [ " price " ], " value " : qty * q [ " price " ], " day_change " : qty * ( q . get ( " change " ) or 0 ), " day_pct " : q . get ( " changePercent " ) or 0 , }) total = sum ( r [ " value " ] for r in rows ) print ( f ' { " symbol " : < 9 }{ " ccy " : < 5 }{ " qty " : > 8 }{ " price " : > 12 }{ " value " : > 14 }{ " day " : > 12 }{ " weight " : > 8 } ' ) for r in sorted ( rows , key = lambda r : - r [ " value " ]): print ( f ' { r [ " symbol " ] : < 9 }{ r [ " currency " ] : < 5 }{ r [ " qty " ] : > 8 }{ r [ " price " ] : > 12 ,. 2 f } ' f ' { r [ " value " ] : > 14 ,. 2 f }{ r [ " day_change " ] : >+ 12 ,. 2 f }{ r [ " value " ] / total : > 8.1 % } ' ) print ( f ' total (mixed currencies): { total : ,. 2 f } ' ) Values are in each symbol's own currency, so VOD.L is in GBp and SAP.DE in EUR; add the EURUSD=X and GBPUSD=X symbols to the same run and multiply if you want one base currency. Wrap the script in a cron entry for 22:30 UTC on weekdays, or save the input as a task in the Apify Console and schedule it there, then read the newest dataset from your code. The same call with curl No Python at hand? The synchronous endpoint runs the Actor and returns the dataset in one request: curl -sS -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/highbrow_fame~yahoo-finance-quotes/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"symbols": ["AAPL", "BTC-USD"], "includeHistory": true, "historyRange": "1mo"}' Add &format=csv to the URL for a spreadsheet-ready response. Cost per 1,000 symbols The Actor charges $0.001 per symbol delivered on the free Apify plan, which is $1.00 per 1,000 symbols, falling to $0.70 per 1,000 on Gold and higher plans. The price is the same with or without history and company data, and unknown symbols are not charged. The seven-symbol quote run at the top costs $0.007; a 500-symbol watchlist refreshed every trading day costs $0.50 a day. Try it with the prefilled input: https://apify.com/highbrow_fame/yahoo-finance-quotes More copy-paste examples (Python, n8n workflow, LangChain tool): Yahoo Finance integration examples on GitHub

title: Ollama: Run LLMs Locally and Swap Them Into Your App With One base_url Change
author: M.T.Ramkrushna
summary: This week's AI tool: Ollama , the simplest way I know to run open-weight LLMs on your own machine and call them from code. Why it's worth 15 minutes of your time: most of the LLM calls you make while building (trying prompts, running unit tests, iterating on a parser) don't need a frontier model. They need something fast, free, and available offline. Ollama gives you that, and because it speaks an OpenAI-compatible API, the same client code can point at a local model in dev and a hosted model in production. Here's exactly how to use it. 1. Install and pull a model On Linux: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh On macOS and Windows, download the app from ollama.com/download . Then pull a model from the model library and chat with it: ollama pull llama3.2 ollama run llama3.2 A few commands you'll use daily: ollama list # models you've downloaded ollama ps # models currently loaded in memory ollama rm llama3.2 # free the disk space How big a model can you run? The Ollama README gives this rule of thumb: at least 8 GB of RAM for 7B models, 16 GB for 13B, and 32 GB for 33B. Start small (a 3B model) and move up only if quality isn't enough for your task. 2. Call it from Python Ollama runs a local server at http://localhost:11434 . The official Python library is the most direct way in: pip install ollama from ollama import chat response = chat ( model = " llama3.2 " , messages = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " Explain idempotency in one sentence. " }], ) print ( response . message . content ) 3. Or keep your OpenAI client and change one line Ollama also exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at /v1 . If your app already uses the OpenAI SDK, you don't rewrite anything: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI ( base_url = " http://localhost:11434/v1 " , api_key = " ollama " , # required by the SDK, ignored by Ollama ) resp = client . chat . completions . create ( model = " llama3.2 " , messages = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " Summarize: the deploy failed because the DB migration timed out. " }], ) print ( resp . choices [ 0 ]. message . content ) Put base_url and model in config, and the same code runs against a local model on your laptop and a hosted model in production. 4. Get structured output you can validate Free-text answers are hard to test. Ollama supports structured outputs : pass a JSON schema in format and the model's reply is constrained to it. Pair it with Pydantic: from ollama import chat from pydantic import BaseModel class Ticket ( BaseModel ): category : str priority : str summary : str response = chat ( model = " llama3.2 " , messages = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " Customer says checkout returns a 500 error since this morning. " }], format = Ticket . model_json_schema (), options = { " temperature " : 0 }, ) ticket = Ticket . model_validate_json ( response . message . content ) print ( ticket ) Setting temperature to 0 makes runs more repeatable, which matters when the output feeds a test. 5. Pin your settings in a Modelfile Instead of repeating the system prompt and parameters everywhere, bake them into a named model with a Modelfile : FROM llama3.2 PARAMETER temperature 0 SYSTEM You classify support tickets. Reply only with the requested JSON. ollama create ticket-bot -f Modelfile ollama run ticket-bot Now every teammate gets the same model, prompt, and parameters by name, and the Modelfile lives in version control next to your code. The workflow I'd use Here's a hypothetical setup for a support-ticket classifier, to show how the pieces fit: Local dev: base_url points at Ollama with a small model. You iterate on prompts and parsing as often as you like, offline, with no API bill. Tests: the Pydantic schema plus temperature 0 give you outputs you can assert on (valid JSON, allowed categories). Production: change base_url and model in config to your hosted provider. The code doesn't change. Before shipping: run the same eval set against the production model, because a small local model passing isn't proof the big one behaves the same way (and vice versa). Where Ollama is not the answer Quality-critical answers: small local models are weaker than frontier models. Use them for dev loops and simple tasks, not as a silent drop-in for hard reasoning. Serving many users: Ollama is built for running models on a machine you control. For high-traffic production serving, look at dedicated inference servers or hosted APIs. Hardware limits: if a model doesn't fit in memory it will be slow or won't load. Check ollama ps and pick a smaller model. References Ollama website and model library Ollama on GitHub (README, install, RAM guidance) OpenAI compatibility docs Structured outputs announcement Modelfile reference ollama-python library What do you use local models for today: dev loops, tests, privacy-sensitive data, or not at all yet?

title: I was tired of letting the OOM killer do my VRAM math, so I wrote a one-file CLI
author: TECHDEV
summary: My workflow for trying a new local model used to be: download 4 GB, watch the progress bar, then read failed to allocate 3412 MiB like it was a fortune cookie. The math that would have saved me fits on a napkin — weights, plus KV cache, plus overhead — but nobody does it before downloading, because the tools that do it live in a browser tab and want you to type in the parameter count by hand. The file is sitting right there on your disk. It knows its own parameter count. So I wrote ggufit : one Python file, standard library only, no install. Point it at a .gguf file and it reads the actual header — tensor table, quantization types, layer count, KV heads — and answers the only question that matters: $ python3 ggufit.py llama-3.1-8b-q4_k_m.gguf --gpu "RTX 4060" ... Verdict: TIGHT — only 0.14 GB headroom; one Chrome tab away from OOM Two things most calculators get wrong, fixed here: KV cache is not a footnote. At 32k context, an 8B model's KV cache costs as much as its weights. ggufit computes it from the real architecture (GQA-aware, so small-kv-head models get the smaller number they deserve). Your 8 GB card doesn't have 8 GB free. The database compares against usable VRAM after driver/display/OS reserve, not the number on the box. Haven't downloaded the model yet? That's the best use case: $ python3 ggufit.py --params 8B --quant q4_k_m --ctx 32768 --gpu "RTX 4060" Verdict: WON'T FIT — short by 3.36 GB try: shorten context to ~5160 tokens (7.39 GB total) try: offload ~80% of layers to CPU/RAM (keep ~6 of 32 on GPU) It also does --table (verdict against every card in the DB), --json with exit code 2 on won't-fit so you can chain it in front of llama-server , and --list-gpus . The weights number is measured from the file; everything estimated is labeled as estimated, because a guess wearing a lab coat is still a guess. Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/ggufit — MIT, PRs welcome, especially new cards for the database (vendor spec sheet numbers only, please).

title: Why Decimal Can Round a UInt256 Token Amount, and an Exact Alternative
author: BlockVectra
summary: The documented raw balance is a UInt256String: an unsigned integer string that can reach 78 digits. When you display one in Python, Decimal looks like the obvious tool. The trap is subtle: building a Decimal from a string is exact, but arithmetic on it can round. Where the rounding happens Decimal(raw) keeps every digit, because construction ignores the context precision. Operations such as scaleb , normalize , multiplication, or division round their result to the context precision, which defaults to 28 significant digits. That holds even at scale 0, where you intend no change at all. The proof below takes the maximum UInt256 value and runs it through scaleb(0).normalize() with precision set to 28 inside localcontext() . The global context is not mutated. The result keeps the leading digits and replaces the rest with zeros, and nothing raises an error. This does not make Decimal the wrong tool. Decimal calculations need a context appropriate to the inputs and operations. For this display-only task, integer formatting avoids depending on that context. Exact integer formatting Python integers have arbitrary precision. int(raw) parses the string exactly, and divmod(value, 10 ** decimals) splits the whole and fractional parts with no rounding. The remainder is left-padded to decimals digits, trailing zeros are stripped, and the parts are joined. No Decimal context is involved in this formatting step. from decimal import Decimal , localcontext def to_display_amount ( raw : str , decimals : int | None ) -> str : if decimals is None : return raw # no decimals metadata: keep the raw integer value = int ( raw ) # parse the decimal string exactly whole , remainder = divmod ( value , 10 ** decimals ) fraction = str ( remainder ). rjust ( decimals , " 0 " ). rstrip ( " 0 " ) return f " { whole } . { fraction } " if fraction else str ( whole ) raw = " 115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457584007913129639935 " with localcontext () as context : context . prec = 28 rounded = format ( Decimal ( raw ). scaleb ( 0 ). normalize (), " f " ) assert rounded != raw # Arithmetic rounded an exact Decimal input. assert to_display_amount ( raw , 0 ) == raw assert to_display_amount ( raw , None ) == raw # Raw units; the scale is still unknown. assert to_display_amount ( raw , 18 ) == " 115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457.584007913129639935 " print ( " rounded: " , rounded ) print ( " exact: " , to_display_amount ( raw , 0 )) print ( " PASS: 4 offline assertions; no network requests " ) On Python 3.14.8 this exits with status 0, makes no network requests, and passes four assertions: the Decimal path differs from the input, scale 0 returns the exact string, None returns the raw string, and scale 18 yields the expected 18-digit fraction. Nullable scale The documented decimals value is an integer from 0 to 255, or null. When it is None , the formatter returns the raw integer string unchanged. That output is in raw units. It is not a scaled amount, and the scale is still unknown, so label it as raw instead of assuming 18. Limits The formatter assumes the input is already a valid unsigned integer string under the documented UInt256String format. It is a formatter, not a validator, so check input at your boundary first. The field definitions are in the wallet assets guide , and the standalone function is in this gist .

title: Subscription Fatigue vs. Ownership Revival in 2026: Your Practical Guide to What Truly Saves You Money
author: Baba Yaga
summary: Subscription Fatigue vs. Ownership Revival in 2026: Your Practical Guide to What Truly Saves You Money Original Engineering Publication: Subscription Fatigue vs. Ownership Revival in 2026: Your Practical Guide to What Truly Saves You Money on shahrukhalid.com Author: Huda Al-Thani | Category: Comparison Content Architectural Deep Dive & Practical Guide The year 2026 finds many of us standing at a financial crossroads, grappling with a silent drain on our wallets: the ever-proliferating world of subscriptions. The year 2026 finds many of us standing at a financial crossroads, grappling with a silent drain on our wallets: the ever-proliferating world of subscriptions. What once promised convenience and affordability has, for many, morphed into a dizzying array of recurring charges that are increasingly difficult to track and even harder to justify. This isn't just a feeling; it's a documented phenomenon known as subscription fatigue, and it's prompting a significant re-evaluation of how we acquire and consume goods and services. A striking 73% of Americans report experiencing this exhaustion from managing numerous recurring charges across everything from streaming and music to software and fitness. The financial impact is profound, with the average US household spending approximately $273 per month on subscriptions in 2026 – a figure consumers often underestimate, believing they spend closer to $86. This "perception gap" highlights a hidden financial drain, pushing us to ask: is it time to reclaim control and embrace the long-term value of ownership once more? Understanding the true Subscription vs Ownership Cost is no longer a niche financial exercise; it's a critical skill for navigating our modern economy and truly saving money. The Architectural Showdown: Core Philosophies & Overview Imagine your personal finances as a meticulously designed structure. Every decision you make about how you acquire goods and services acts as a foundational pillar, shaping its stability and long-term resilience. For years, the "subscription" pillar seemed like the ultimate innovation – a sleek, agile solution to access anything, anytime, without the burden of upfront costs. We were promised a future of effortless access, where the latest software, an endless library of entertainment, or even a vehicle could be yours with a simple monthly payment. This "access over ownership" paradigm became the dominant architectural philosophy for many aspects of our lives. It felt liberating: no large capital outlay, always updated, and the flexibility to cancel if your needs changed. The idea was to rent the utility, not own the asset. This philosophy champions agility, low barriers to entry, and continuous innovation delivered directly to you. However, as with any grand architectural design, unforeseen challenges have emerged. That once-sleek pillar of subscriptions has started to feel less like a single, strong support and more like a dense thicket of fragile, intertwined vines, each demanding its own care and feeding. This is the heart of what we call "subscription fatigue." It's not just about having a few streaming services; it's about the cumulative weight of dozens of recurring payments for everything from niche apps to smart home features, all vying for our attention and our dollars. The exhaustion stems from managing numerous recurring charges across various services like streaming, music, software, and fitness. This phenomenon is very real and widely felt, with a significant majority of Americans – 73% – reporting they are experiencing it in 2026. This isn't a mere annoyance; it's a tangible stressor that impacts household budgets and mental bandwidth. The financial implications are staggering. The average US household is now shelling out approximately $273 per month on subscriptions in 2026. What’s truly alarming is that this figure is often severely underestimated by consumers, who typically believe their monthly spend is closer to a mere $86. This colossal "perception gap" – a difference of nearly $200 – highlights a hidden financial drain that quietly erodes savings and financial peace of mind. Many of these costs are for "zombie subscriptions" – services we signed up for and forgot about, continuing to drain funds for unused access. Forgotten renewals and these phantom charges are a major contributor to the financial burden. Moreover, the constant drumbeat of price increases across services only exacerbates the financial burden and frustration, making it harder to keep a stable budget. In response to this growing fatigue, a powerful counter-movement is gaining momentum: the "Ownership Revival." This philosophy champions stability, long-term value, and complete control over one's assets. It's a return to the idea that some things are simply better to own outright, providing a sense of permanence and an escape from the endless cycle of recurring payments. The ownership revival isn't about rejecting all subscriptions; it's about discerning when ownership truly offers superior value. It's a shift from the transient nature of access back to the enduring benefits of possession. For instance, consider the automotive industry. While car subscription services offer flexibility, consumers are increasingly pushing back against the idea of features like heated seats being locked behind ongoing subscriptions in vehicles they technically "own." BMW, for example, publicly acknowledged this sentiment, reversing their decision to charge subscriptions for heated seats in certain regions. This pushback is a clear indicator of the burgeoning desire for ownership economy benefits – a desire for features and functionalities to be inherent to the purchased product, not an additional, ongoing cost. The core tension in this architectural showdown lies in two fundamentally different approaches to value. Subscriptions offer immediate gratification, flexibility, and a lower upfront Subscription vs Ownership Cost , but can lead to an escalating long-term cost and a feeling of perpetual indebtedness. Ownership demands a higher initial investment but promises greater control, potential for asset appreciation (or at least predictable depreciation), and freedom from recurring financial commitments. For a general reader, understanding this philosophical divide is the first step in making smarter financial decisions. It’s about recognizing that while subscriptions have their place, they are not a universal panacea for all needs. The goal of this guide is to equip you with the practical tools and insights needed to navigate this complex landscape, identify Subscription model alternatives , and ultimately find Subscription fatigue solutions that genuinely save you money. We'll delve into the nuances of Cost of ownership vs subscription , helping you determine Is ownership cheaper than subscription in various scenarios, and uncover effective strategies for Saving money subscriptions vs buying . This isn't just about cutting costs; it's about making conscious choices that align with your long-term financial well-being and personal values. title: Task Manager on Mac: How to Monitor Processes and Fix Slow Apps
author: zprostudio
summary: If you've recently switched from Windows to Mac, you might wonder where the Task Manager is. The good news is that macOS already includes a similar tool called Activity Monitor. You can use it to check running processes, investigate high CPU or memory usage, monitor energy consumption, and troubleshoot applications that stop responding. In this guide, we'll look at how to open Activity Monitor and use it safely. Does Mac Have a Task Manager? Yes, macOS has a built-in alternative called Activity Monitor. While Windows users are familiar with Task Manager, Mac users can use Activity Monitor to view details about running processes and system resource usage. It includes five useful areas: CPU: Shows processor usage by applications and processes. Memory: Displays memory consumption. Energy: Helps identify applications with a high energy impact. Disk: Shows disk activity. Network: Displays network activity. For most everyday troubleshooting, Activity Monitor is a good place to start. How to Open Activity Monitor on Mac You don't need to download or install anything. Follow these steps: Press Command + Space to open Spotlight Search. Enter Activity Monitor. Press Return. Open the application and select the tab you need. Alternatively, navigate to Applications → Utilities → Activity Monitor. How to Identify Apps Using Too Much CPU Does your Mac become slow when you open a particular application? Try this: Open Activity Monitor. Select the CPU tab. Click the CPU column to sort processes by usage. Look for applications consuming unusually high resources. Check whether the usage continues even after the demanding task has finished. Keep in mind that high CPU usage isn't always a sign of trouble. Tasks such as video rendering, gaming, and software compilation can naturally require significant processing power. Investigate the process before deciding to close it. How to Check Memory Usage If your Mac feels sluggish when multiple applications are open, the Memory tab can help you investigate. Look for applications that consistently consume substantial memory, and consider whether the overall memory situation corresponds with the slowdown. Important: macOS manages memory dynamically. Seeing a large amount of memory in use doesn't automatically mean your Mac has a problem. Focus on the overall situation rather than closing applications simply because they appear near the top of the list. How to Check Battery Usage MacBook users can also use Activity Monitor to investigate unexpected battery drain. Open the Energy tab and review the applications with a high energy impact. If one application stands out, consider whether it is performing a demanding task or behaving unexpectedly. You can then close it normally or investigate further if the issue continues. How to Force Quit a Frozen App When an application stops responding, macOS provides a quick way to close it. Option 1: Use the keyboard shortcut Press Command + Option + Escape. Select the unresponsive application. Click Force Quit. Option 2: Use Activity Monitor Open Activity Monitor. Find the relevant application or process. Select it. Click the Stop button in the toolbar. Choose Quit first when appropriate. Use Force Quit if necessary. Be careful: force quitting may result in unsaved work being lost. What Should You Avoid Closing? Not every process you see in Activity Monitor is an ordinary application. Some processes are essential to macOS or support other applications. Closing an unfamiliar process can cause unexpected behavior. Before terminating a process: Check what the process belongs to. Consider whether it is performing a legitimate task. Try quitting the application normally first. Avoid terminating unfamiliar system processes without understanding their purpose. If an application repeatedly freezes, check for software updates and investigate the application rather than repeatedly forcing it to close. A Simple Mac Troubleshooting Checklist When your Mac becomes slow, follow this workflow: Identify whether the entire Mac is slow or only one app. Open Activity Monitor using Spotlight. Check CPU usage. Review memory usage. Check Energy if battery life is the concern. Identify the application responsible. Quit the app normally if possible. Force quit only when necessary. Restart your Mac if the problem continues. This approach helps you investigate the cause instead of randomly closing processes. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Mac equivalent of Windows Task Manager? Activity Monitor is the built-in macOS equivalent for inspecting running processes and system resource usage. Can I open Activity Monitor with a keyboard shortcut? Yes. Press Command + Space, type Activity Monitor, and press Return. Is Activity Monitor safe to use? Yes, it is a built-in macOS utility. However, you should be careful when terminating processes you don't recognize. Should I force quit an app that uses a lot of CPU? Not necessarily. Some applications need significant CPU resources for demanding tasks. Investigate whether the usage is expected before force quitting. Conclusion Activity Monitor is one of the most useful built-in tools for Mac troubleshooting. It helps you understand CPU usage, memory consumption, energy impact, and running processes without installing a separate task manager. Start by identifying the problem, check the relevant information, and close applications carefully. For more practical technology tutorials and troubleshooting guides, visit ZProStudio. title: I Built a Face Shape Detector That Shows Its Work — and Keeps Going
author: KnowYourFaceShape
summary: Most face shape tools give you a label and a list of haircuts. I wanted to build the opposite: something that shows the five measurements behind the label, then keeps going into the questions people actually have afterwards. Try it here: knowyourfaceshape.com — free, no sign-up, and your photo never leaves your browser. What it does You can get your face shape three ways: upload a photo, take a 60-second quiz, or enter four tape-measure readings. The photo path runs MediaPipe Face Landmarker on your device, takes ten landmarks, builds five ratios — face length, forehead, jaw, jaw angle and chin taper — and compares them against a published prototype table for seven shapes: oval, round, square, oblong, heart, diamond and triangle. The part I care about comes next. Each result links to a shape guide, hairstyle breakdowns written against the same measurements, and sizing calculators for glasses frames, hats, earrings and necklaces. There's an AI attractiveness test on the site now too, and more tools are on the way. Tech stack React 19, MediaPipe tasks-vision running inside a Web Worker, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Inference happens on your device, so there is no photo upload and nothing for me to store. Two things that were harder than expected MediaPipe normalizes x by image width and y by image height, which means the same face measures differently in a landscape photo than a portrait one until you undo it. And resisting the urge to print an accuracy percentage was its own challenge. The site publishes the full rule set and every threshold instead, so you can check the call against your own numbers. Why I built it Because a lot of face shape content online ends in a product recommendation. This site sells nothing and recommends no brand. What's next A shareable result card and a hairstyle matcher are first in line, along with more measuring tools. Would love feedback from anyone who tries it — especially if you land on a borderline result and disagree with the shape. Tell me which measurement looked off and I'll dig in.

title: How to Unhide Apps on iPhone: A Step-by-Step Guide
author: zprostudio
summary: Have you ever searched your iPhone for an app and found that its icon was missing? It can be confusing, especially when you know the app was installed previously. The good news is that a missing app isn't always deleted. It may be hidden, removed from the Home Screen, placed on a hidden page, restricted by Screen Time, or waiting to be downloaded again. In this guide, you'll learn how to find and unhide apps on your iPhone using simple steps. Why Is an App Missing from Your iPhone? Before changing any settings, it's useful to understand what might have happened. Common reasons include: The app was removed from the Home Screen. The entire Home Screen page was hidden. The app was hidden using Apple's app privacy feature. Screen Time restrictions made an app unavailable. The app was deleted or offloaded. The app was hidden from App Store purchase history. Each situation has a different solution, so start with the method that best matches your problem. Method 1: Find an App in the App Library If an app is installed but no longer appears on your Home Screen, check the App Library first. Steps Go to your iPhone's Home Screen. Swipe left past all Home Screen pages. Continue until you reach the App Library. Find the app by browsing the categories or using the App Library search. Touch and hold the app icon. If the option is available, drag the app to your preferred Home Screen page. This method works when an app has been removed from the Home Screen but remains installed. Important: Apps hidden with Apple's dedicated Hidden feature in iOS 18 and later generally won't appear in normal Search results or the usual App Library categories. For those apps, use Method 2. Method 2: Unhide an App from the Hidden Folder Apple introduced a dedicated app-hiding feature in iOS 18. When you hide a compatible app, it moves to the Hidden folder in the App Library and requires authentication to access. Step-by-step instructions Step 1: Open your iPhone's Home Screen. Step 2: Swipe left past all your Home Screen pages to reach the App Library. Step 3: Scroll down to the Hidden folder. Step 4: Tap the folder and authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID, or your iPhone passcode. Step 5: Touch and hold the app you want to restore. Step 6: Select Don't Require Face ID or the equivalent option shown on your device, then authenticate if requested. The app is no longer hidden and appears in the App Library. If you want its icon on your Home Screen, you can move it there. You can also check Settings → Apps → Hidden Apps on supported iOS versions to view the list of hidden apps after authentication. Method 3: Unhide a Home Screen Page If multiple app icons disappeared at once, you may have hidden a whole Home Screen page. How to restore it Touch and hold an empty area on the Home Screen. Tap Edit. Choose Edit Pages, or tap the dots near the bottom of the screen. Look for pages with unchecked circles. Tap the circle for the page you want to display. Tap Done. The page and its apps should become visible again. This method is especially useful when you remember having several apps in one place but can't find any of them on your current Home Screen. Method 4: Check Screen Time Settings Screen Time can restrict access to certain apps and features. This is worth checking if a built-in app, such as Safari, has disappeared or become unavailable. Steps to follow Open Settings. Tap Screen Time. Select Content & Privacy Restrictions. Review the available app, feature, and content restrictions. Adjust the relevant setting if you have permission to do so. The exact options depend on your iOS version and configuration. If the iPhone belongs to a child or is managed by a school or organization, you may need the authorized parent or administrator to make the change. Method 5: Restore an App from the App Store If an app was deleted, you may need to reinstall it. If you previously hid it from your App Store purchase history, you may need to unhide the purchase first. What to do Open the App Store. Tap your account picture. Open your Apple Account settings and look for Hidden Purchases, where available. Unhide the relevant purchase. Return to the App Store and download the app if necessary. Use the Apple Account associated with the original purchase. An app may also be unavailable if it has been removed from the store or no longer supports your device. Unhiding an App Store purchase and unhiding an app on your device are two different actions. Quick Troubleshooting Table Problem What to try App icon missing from Home Screen Check the App Library App hidden with Face ID Open the Hidden folder Several icons missing together Restore the hidden Home Screen page Built-in app unavailable Review Screen Time restrictions App was deleted Redownload from the App Store App doesn't appear in purchase history Check the correct Apple Account Common Mistakes to Avoid Searching repeatedly for a privacy-hidden app: Apps in the Hidden folder aren't normally discoverable through Search. Open the folder directly. Resetting the iPhone too soon: Check the App Library, hidden pages, and restrictions before considering a reset. Confusing purchase hiding with app hiding: Hiding an App Store purchase doesn't automatically hide the installed app, and unhiding a purchase doesn't necessarily reinstall it. Changing restrictions without permission: If a device is managed by a parent or organization, follow the appropriate approval process. Frequently Asked Questions Can I unhide apps without deleting them? Yes. If an app is hidden or simply removed from the Home Screen, you can usually restore its visibility without deleting it. Why can't I find a hidden app using Search? When an app is hidden through Apple's privacy feature, it is excluded from normal Search results. Open the Hidden folder in the App Library instead. Will unhiding an app put it back on the Home Screen? Removing an app's hidden status makes it available in the App Library. You may still need to move its icon to the Home Screen. Do I need to reset my iPhone to restore missing apps? Usually not. Try the methods above first. A reset is not the normal solution for a hidden app. Conclusion Learning how to unhide apps on iPhone can save you time and help you avoid unnecessary troubleshooting. Start by checking the App Library, then look in the Hidden folder, restore any hidden Home Screen pages, review Screen Time, and reinstall the app only if needed. The key is identifying why the app disappeared before changing your settings. For more practical technology tutorials and easy-to-follow troubleshooting guides, explore ZProStudio.

title: Peering Inside the Black Box: How Mechanistic Interpretability is Decoding AI Minds
author: Mecky Alvin Tanuwidjaya
summary: Peering inside the black box: Mapping the internal neural circuits of large language models. Why reverse-engineering neural networks down to individual circuits is the ultimate key to AI safety, alignment, and trust. For years, the artificial intelligence community accepted a fundamental tradeoff: as neural networks became more powerful, they also became more opaque. Large Language Models (LLMs) with hundreds of billions of parameters perform stunning feats of reasoning, coding, and synthesis, yet even the engineers who built them cannot pinpoint the exact mathematical paths a model took to reach a specific answer. We have built systems that work brilliantly, but operate as complete "black boxes." In high-stakes domains—such as healthcare, autonomous defense, and corporate governance—relying on a system you cannot inspect is a massive liability. To solve this, researchers at leading AI labs are pioneering a new scientific discipline: Mechanistic Interpretability. What is Mechanistic Interpretability? If classical AI evaluation is like giving a student a standardized multiple-choice test, Mechanistic Interpretability is like performing an MRI scan on the brain while the student solves the problem. Instead of treating an AI model as an unbreakable black box and evaluating only its final text output, Mechanistic Interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer the weights, neurons, and attention heads inside a trained model. Researchers break down the neural network into human-understandable algorithms and logic circuits—much like software engineers decompile complex machine code back into readable programming logic. Through techniques like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), researchers can now identify specific "features" inside a model—pinpointing the exact group of artificial neurons that fire when the AI thinks about concepts like deceit, specific geography, computer code syntax, or ethical dilemmas. Why Mapping the AI Mind Changes Everything Decoding the internal representations of large AI models transforms how we build, align, and secure artificial intelligence: Detecting Hidden Deception Before Deployment Standard safety evaluations rely on checking model outputs. However, if an advanced model learns to be deceptively aligned—behaving well during testing but acting maliciously when deployed—traditional testing will miss it. Mechanistic Interpretability allows safety researchers to look directly at the internal state of the model to see if "deceptive thoughts" or manipulation features are active, catching dangerous behavior before software is released. Surgical Model Editing Without Retraining When a traditional LLM exhibits a dangerous bias, hallucination, or safety flaw, developers usually have to spend millions of dollars fine-tuning the entire model or adding clumsy system prompts. With mechanistic mapping, engineers can perform "neural surgery"—directly targeting and turning down the specific weight parameters responsible for the bad behavior without degrading the rest of the model's capabilities. Moving from Empirical Guesswork to True Science For the past decade, deep learning has been largely empirical: engineers tweaked hyperparameters, added more training data, and hoped for the best. Mechanistic Interpretability shifts machine learning from trial-and-error alchemy into a rigorous, verifiable science where every emergent behavior can be mathematically explained. The Frontier of AI Safety We are entering an era where building safe AI isn't just about training bigger models or adding external guardrails. It is about understanding the fundamental machinery of artificial thought. By opening the black box and mapping the inner workings of neural networks, Mechanistic Interpretability ensures that as AI systems grow exponentially more capable, humanity retains the tools needed to keep them transparent, predictable, and aligned with human values.

title: Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too.
author: TECHDEV
summary: Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too. Last month my team reversed a queue decision. Nobody could say why we had picked the first design, what evidence it rested on, or who had signed off on the replacement. The old design was still half-wired in as a "fallback", quietly depending on the thing we had just replaced. We found out in production. Vector RAG remembers text . It does not remember decisions — what was chosen, what it rested on, what contradicted it, and what replaced it. So I built a tiny local graph for exactly that: memgraph . What it does One zero-dependency Node.js CLI. No network, no server, no embeddings. The store is a single JSON file you can commit next to your code. memgraph init memgraph add --type decision --title "Use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for the queue" --source "ADR-014" memgraph add --type fact --title "NOTIFY payloads cap at 8000 bytes" --source "Postgres docs" memgraph link m-002 m-001 --relation contradicts memgraph add --type decision --title "Switch the queue to Redis Streams" --source "ADR-019" memgraph supersede m-001 m-003 --reason "payload cap makes NOTIFY the wrong tool" Three questions it answers, fast: Why did we decide this? memgraph why m-003 — source, supporters, contradictions, supersession. Is anything stale or contradictory? memgraph check — unresolved contradictions, live nodes resting on superseded ones, sourceless claims. What do we believe? memgraph list — every node, with superseded ones marked. memgraph check exits 1 when it finds an error, so it works as a CI gate: a PR that introduces a contradiction, or keeps depending on a superseded decision, fails before it merges. Demo The repo ships a small team graph — a queue decision, the fact that killed it, its replacement, and one leftover fallback still depending on the dead design: sh examples/run-demo.sh memgraph check on that graph reports exactly two problems: the fallback reader depends on a superseded decision, and one open question has no source. The contradiction between the payload-cap fact and the old decision does not get flagged — the old decision was superseded, so that contradiction is resolved history, not a live conflict. One honesty note A graph is only as good as what you record. memgraph cannot tell you whether a source is true — it tells you where every claim came from and whether the graph still holds together. A decision with no source is a rumor with formatting; that is why check flags it. And when a decision changes, supersede it — don't delete it. Deleting history is how teams end up re-litigating the same choice every six months. Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/memgraph — MIT, zero dependencies, Node.js 18+.

title: SlothAI: Offline, Open-Source AI Tools for the Gloriously Lazy 🦥
author: ANKIT KUMAR
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Meet SlothAI 🦥 — an offline, local-first web companion designed for anyone who believes sloths have life figured out. Instead of paying recurring cloud subscriptions or giving away personal correspondence to remote servers, SlothAI runs open-weight models (like Llama 3.2 ) locally on your hardware via Ollama . It packages 6 micro-tools dedicated to taking over the tedious mental chores that drain your energy throughout the day: 📝 TL;DR Machine — Summarizes long emails and articles into 2–3 key bullet points so you never read fluff again. ✉️ Ghost Writer — Transforms rough bullet points into polished, tone-adjusted emails and messages in seconds. 🎲 The Decider — Eliminates decision fatigue by making definitive, reasoned choices (no endless debates). 🛋️ Lazy Planner — Reorganizes overwhelming to-do lists into relaxed schedules with built-in rest breaks. 😴 Bedtime Story — Generates peaceful, offline bedtime stories to help you wind down without screens. 💬 Smart Reply — Instantly drafts 3 ready-to-send responses: Casual 🙂, Professional 💼, and Witty 😄. Who gets to be lazier because of it? Anyone suffering from modern cognitive overload: developers drowning in Slack messages, students tired of drafting polite emails, or anyone who just wants to close their laptop and take a nap without leaving unfinished mental tasks hanging. Demo grandsonofsitaram.github.io Quick Local Run: Clone the repo and run python -m http.server 3000 Run ollama run llama3.2 Open http://localhost:3000 — that's it! Code https://github.com/GRANDSONOFSITARAM/slothai The entire project is built with zero framework bloat: Zero build steps: Pure HTML5, CSS3, and modern vanilla JavaScript. Zero external client libraries: No React, no Vite, no node_modules. Under 40 KB total: Blazing fast load times, instant startup, and runs straight from disk. How I Built It SlothAI was built around the principle of open-source local inference: 1. The Open-Weight Core: Ollama + Llama 3.2 The AI engine runs entirely on Ollama , an open-source framework that runs quantized open-weight GGUF models directly on consumer CPUs and GPUs. We utilize Llama 3.2 (3.2B / 1B), Meta's open-weight model optimized for edge devices and low-latency instruction following. Any open model supported by Ollama works out-of-the-box: Mistral , Gemma 2 , Phi-3 , or Qwen 2.5 . SlothAI auto-detects installed models via /api/tags and populates them in a single-click dropdown. 2. Client-Side NDJSON Streaming Rather than waiting for full completions, SlothAI streams responses directly into the DOM using an asynchronous generator over Ollama’s /api/chat endpoint: async * streamChat ( messages , model , options = {}) { const res = await fetch ( ` ${ this . host } /api/chat` , { method : ' POST ' , headers : { ' Content-Type ' : ' application/json ' }, body : JSON . stringify ({ model , messages , stream : true , options }) }); const reader = res . body . getReader (); const decoder = new TextDecoder (); // Decode and yield NDJSON tokens in real-time } Tokens render live with a blinking cursor and typewriter fluidity, giving real-time feedback with zero latency. 3. Glassmorphism Design System Built from scratch with CSS custom properties, responsive grid/flex layouts, keyboard shortcuts ( Ctrl+Enter to generate, Esc to cancel), animated ambient gradient orbs, and copy-to-clipboard functionality. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open-source AI isn't just an alternative to closed APIs; for a utility like SlothAI, open innovation is the only architecture that makes sense : 🔒 Absolute Privacy by Architecture : To summarize private emails, draft sensitive work messages, or plan daily routines, users shouldn't have to beam personal life data to proprietary cloud servers where it might be logged or used to train third-party models. With open-weight models, your data never leaves your laptop. 📴 True Offline Capability (Zero Internet Needed) : Closed APIs turn your software into a useless brick the moment WiFi drops or you step on an airplane. Open-weight inference runs completely offline. Once your weights are on your SSD, you can generate bedtime stories or write emails in an off-grid cabin. 💰 Zero Subscription & Zero Token Anxiety : Closed LLM APIs introduce rate limits, credit cards, and per-token anxiety. With open models, inference costs exactly \$0. Run 10 tokens or 100,000 tokens — you never get an unexpected bill at the end of the month. 🔄 Freedom to Swap & Hack : No vendor lock-in. Want a smaller 0.5B model for an old laptop? Swap it. Want a specialized uncensored model or domain-specific fine-tune? Just pull it. Every prompt is transparently editable in app.js . The Lazy Payoff Here is the actual mental energy SlothAI saves in a typical week: Drafting routine emails : 8 minutes → 15 seconds with Ghost Writer. Catching up on 50-message Slack threads : 5 minutes → 10 seconds with TL;DR Machine. Deciding dinner / weekend plans : 10+ minutes of deliberation → 5 seconds with The Decider. Structuring tomorrow’s chaotic to-do list : 15 minutes → 20 seconds with Lazy Planner. That adds up to over 45 minutes saved every single day . More importantly, it eliminates the micro-friction and procrastination of starting tasks. The sloth would be proud. 🦥 Prize Categories Open-Source AI at its Core (runs fully open-weight models via Ollama) Local-First & Offline Innovation (zero internet required, zero cloud leakage)
